WEEK 28 Skill: Cultural Patterns Essential Element 4: Standard 10 A County Fair Map Introducing the Map Explain to students that families have special things they do year after year. It may be a family vacation to a cabin, a holiday celebration at Grandma’s, or watching the fireworks on the 4th of July. T ell students that those are customs. A custom is a group’s special way of doing something. One custom many communities have is a county fair. A county fair is held every year. Ask students if they have ever gone to a county fair. T alk about what they have seen and done at the fair. Explain to students that a county fair may include animals, shows, rides, games, and food. People from the community often enter their handmade goods such as art, crafts, and homegrown fruits and vegetables into a contest. People show the animals they have raised. The animals are judged and receive ribbons. Carnivals and grandstand acts are also parts of a county fair. Show students the county fair map. Point out the different areas shown on the map. T alk about what kinds of things are located in each of these areas. Be sure to read the labels on the map and review the vocabulary words with students throughout the week. Introducing Vocabulary carnival A carnival is a fair with rides and games. county A county is part of a state. States are divided into counties. custom A custom is a special way that people do things. Going to a county fair every year is a custom. entrance An entrance is a way into a place. fair A fair is a show of farm products. A county fair shows animals and has fun things to do. WEEK 29 Skill: Economics Essential Element 4: Standard 11 A Product Map of Kansas Introducing the Map T ell students that states produce or make the food we buy in stores. Sometimes a state is known for the product that it grows or makes. For example, Florida is known for the oranges it grows. Idaho is known for its potatoes. Iowa is known for its hogs and corn. T alk about how farmers grow crops and raise animals to feed the world. T ell students that each farmer produces enough food to feed more than 80 people. Refer back to Week 19 “A Rural Area Map” to look at a map of the two farms. Show students the product map of Kansas. Explain to students that this is a farm product map. Have students look at the key to see which three crops and which two livestock are important in Kansas. T ell students that Kansas is called “The Wheat State.” It grows more wheat than any other state. Kansas also grows lots of corn and sorghum. Explain that sorghum is a grain that is made into flour, cereals, and food for animals. T ell students that corn, sorghum, and wheat are called crops. Crops are plants that farmers grow to sell. Share with students that Kansas is also called “The Breadbasket of America.” T alk about why the state would have this nickname. Explain to students that corn, sorghum, and wheat are all grains that can be ground into flour for breads. Kansas farmers also raise cattle and hogs. Cattle and hogs are called livestock. Livestock are animals that farmers raise to sell for food. Review vocabulary throughout the week to help students understand the concepts presented in this lesson. Introducing Vocabulary cattle Cattle are cows, bulls, and steers that are raised on a farm or ranch. crop A crop is a plant that farmers grow for food. Wheat is a crop. livestock Livestock are animals raised on a farm or ranch. Cattle are livestock. product map A product map shows where things like crops and livestock are found. state A state is a part of a country. There are 50 states in the United States. WEEK 33 Skill: Tourism Essential Element 5: Standard 15 A Tourist Map of Hawaii Introducing the Map Ask students to name a state they would like to visit and tell why. An example might be the state of California. Students may point out cities they would like to visit such as Los Angeles or Hollywood. California has beautiful beaches along the Pacific Ocean. Disneyland and the San Diego Zoo are popular places. Show students the tourist map of Hawaii. Explain to students that many people like to go to Hawaii because it is a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean. T alk about how Hawaii is made up of eight main islands. Read the names of the islands for students. Refer to Week 16, “A Land and Water Map of Hawaii” for additional information about the islands and how to pronounce their names. Read and discuss the tourist attractions on the island of Oahu. T ell students that this island is where most people fly into. It has the capital of Hawaii. T ell students that Oahu has beautiful beaches. It has the Polynesian Cultural Center. This is where people can learn about the history of Hawaii and the people who settled the islands. People can watch shows at the center, which include hula dancing. People also visit Pearl Harbor to remember those who fought and died in World War II. The ship Arizona is found there. Next, have students look at the big island of Hawaii. Students may get confused that the state is called Hawaii, and so is the biggest island. The big island of Hawaii is famous for its active volcanoes. Kilauea is the most active. Lava flows from the volcano all the time. Visitors can watch the erupting volcano. People visit the V olcanoes National Park to learn about volcanoes. People also go to Parker Ranch, which is the largest beef cattle ranch in Hawaii. Introducing the Map Have students look at the classroom globe and a wall map. T alk about how the two are alike and how they are different. Remind students that a globe is a small model of the round Earth. Since it is round, only one side of a globe can be seen at a time. A map is different because it is a flat picture. T ell students that a map is a drawing of a place as if seen from above. The main purpose of a map is to show where things or places are located. A flat map is easier to carry around or print in a book. A map can show the whole Earth or a close-up view of an area. For example, a map can show the world, a country, a state, a city, or a neighborhood. Explain that maps can show different types of places and things. Maps can also show how far one place is from another. T alk about different kinds of maps that are familiar to the students, such as road maps, tourist maps, maps of shopping malls, or a floor plan of a house. Show students the map of North and South America. T ell students that this flat map shows part of the Earth. T ell students the definition of a continent. Have students name the two continents that are shown. Define ocean for students. Have students name and locate the three oceans on the map. Read the caption with students. Also talk about the four directions shown on the map. You may wish to show students the globe picture from Week 1 for comparison. Remind students to use the map when answering the questions. WEEK 34 Skill: Natural Resources Essential Element 5: Standard 16 A Resource Map of Maine Introducing the Map T ell students that things found in nature are important to people. Materials found in nature are called natural resources. Examples of natural resources are things like water, forests, soil, and minerals. Show students the resource map of Maine. Read and discuss the kinds of things they see on the map and the symbols on the map key. Look at the small map of the United States to see where Maine is located within the United States. Share the following information with students as they study the map: • Maine is called “The Pine Tree State.” Forests cover most of Maine. Maine has the most forests of any state in the U.S. The trees that grow in Maine’s forests are mostly evergreen trees. Names include pine, balsam fir, and spruce. Other trees of Maine are basswood, beech, maple, oak, and white and yellow birch. • Maine has many forest animals. It is famous for its black bears, bobcats, and moose that live in northern Maine. Maine’s state animal is the moose. • Maine borders the Atlantic Ocean. The Atlantic Ocean provides fish, lobsters, and other shellfish for Maine. Kinds of fish caught include cod, flounder, and ocean perch. Maine ranks first in the country for lobsters and soft-shell clams. • Maine has more than 5,000 rivers and streams. Three of the major rivers are shown on the map. Students will notice that the rivers flow into the Atlantic Ocean. • Maine also has mountains. Most of the mountains are forested and look green all year long. From this lesson, students should understand that Maine is rich in natural resources. Waterways and forests are its best natural resources. Review vocabulary throughout the week with students to check for understanding. Introducing Vocabulary forest A forest is a large area thick with trees. natural resources Natural resources are things found in nature that are useful to people. Forests and water are natural resources. waterway A waterway is a body of water that boats travel on. A river or an ocean is a waterway. ANSWER KEY Monday 1. content.passage: 142 Daily Geography Practice • EMC 3711 • © Evan-Moor Corp. WEEK 35 Skill: Interpreting the Past Essential Element 6: Standard 17 Clarksville: Then and Now Introducing the Map T ell students that there are many kinds of maps. Maps show things such as cities, farm products, landforms and waterways, natural resources, and weather. T ell students there is another kind of map. It is called a history map. A history map shows a place as it looked in the past. Show students the maps of Clarksville. T alk about how the top map shows the town of Clarksville in the past. Have students name the kinds of things they see on the map. Students will notice that there are just a few houses. A man is in a wagon pulled by a horse. Life in Clarksville 150 years ago was simple. Students should conclude that Clarksville was probably a farming community. Then have students look at the map of Clarksville today. Havestudents name the kinds of things they see in the town. Have students compare and contrast the two maps. Students should notice things that are the same. For example, the placement of the bridge is in the same area. They should notice changes to the town. For example, Clarksville 150 years ago had a covered wooden bridge. Now, Clarksville has a modern bridge that is probably made of steel. Wagons on dirt roads were seen in the past, and now cars travel on the paved roads. T alk about other changes from the past to the present. Discuss with students what Clarksville might look like in the future. In this lesson, students should begin to understand that history maps help us to learn about the past. They help to plan for the present and for the future. Review the concepts of past, present, and future with students throughout the week. WEEK 3 Skill: Basic Elements Essential Element 1: Standard 1 Directions on a Map Introducing the Map Show students the map of Prentis Park. Give students a few minutes to study the map. Read the title and discuss the different areas of the park. Discuss how maps show directions. T ell students that directions help you locate places. T alk about how some maps have the words north, south, east, and west printed on the sides of the map. Other maps like this one of the park have a compass rose to show directions. T ell students that a compass rose is a symbol that helps them to read a map. The arrows on the compass rose point to the four main directions—north, south, east, and west. T ell students that north is up, south is down, east is to the right, and west is to the left on this map. Define location for the students. Then have students find the location of the different areas in Prentis Park—the entrance, the baseball diamond, the picnic area, the swimming pool, and the playground. Then ask students some questions using directions. Ask if the entrance to the park is in the north or south side of the park. They should recognize that it is located at the top of the map or in the north. Then ask students a harder question. First have them put a finger on the picnic area. Then ask if the swimming pool is east or west of the picnic area. The swimming pool is to the right or the east of the picnic area. You may wish to ask more questions using directions to check for understanding. Be sure to review vocabulary throughout the week. Note that Week 4 also provides students with practice using directions. Introducing Vocabulary compass rose A compass rose is a symbol on a map. It shows directions such as north, south, east, and west. direction A direction tells where something is found. The four main directions are north, south, east, and west. entrance An entrance is a way into a place. location Location is the place where something is found. ANSWER KEY Monday 1. a park 2. Prentis Park Tuesday 1. directions 2. north, south, east, and west Wednesday 1. north 2. playground Thursday 1. east 2. west Friday 1. east 2. playground Challenge Students should color the north arrow red, the south arrow blue, the east arrow yellow, and the west arrow green on the compass rose. 3711BookNoTransp.indb 14 9/21/12 9:43 AM

WEEK 9 Skill: Mental Maps Essential Element 1: Standard 2 Picturing a Place Introducing the Map Ask students to look around the classroom for one minute. Describe the classroom to students while their eyes are closed. Ask them to picture in their minds what their classroom looks like as you describe it. Ask students to open their eyes and look around the classroom again. Then tell students to close their eyes again. Ask them to name different things in the classroom. Have students open their eyes and look around the room. What did they remember? Explain to students that what they just did was to make a picture, or map, of the classroom in their minds. Ask students to think about their home. Ask them to picture in their minds the inside and outside of their home. Where is the kitchen, their bedroom, or a bathroom? Have them think about the outside of their home. What kinds of things are outside? T ell students they have just made a picture in their minds of their home. They have just made a map of their home in their minds. Now, have students look at the map of the classroom. T alk about the different areas of the classroom. Read the caption and follow the directions. Then have students turn the classroom map over. Ask students which things they remembered about the classroom. Make a list of everything they remembered on the board. Then have students turn the map back over to check to see how many things they remembered. Did they also remember where things were located? T ell students that they made a map of the classroom in their minds. Share with students that it is important to make pictures in their minds. Those pictures help them to remember better. Students may find it difficult to understand the concept of mental maps. Students are not expected to define a mental map, but rather begin to understand how making pictures in their minds helps them to remember where things are located. Week 10 also addresses the concept of mental maps. Introducing Vocabulary mental map (not included in the glossary) A mental map is a map that you picture in your mind. WEEK 1 0 Skill: Mental Maps Essential Element 1: Standard 2 Picturing the United States Introducing the Map Ask students to think about their house. Ask them to picture in their minds the inside of their house. T ell them that it helps to close their eyes when they picture something in their minds. Then tell students what they have just done is to make a map of their house. Next, have them think about the neighborhood where they live. Have them take a “walk” through their neighborhood by thinking about the places where they live. They have just made a map of the neighborhood in their minds. Now, ask them to think about something very large—the United States. Show students the classroom map of the United States. T race over the shape with your finger. T alk about how the United States is made up of 50 states. T ell students that all the states together make one big country. Most of the states are close together. T wo states—Alaska and Hawaii—are far away from the others. That is why they have to be in little maps. Help students to find their state within the country. T alk about how their state is a part of the country. Help students to notice that each state is a different shape and size. What shape and size is their state? In this lesson, students take a look at the United States. They look at the size and shape of the country. They also begin to recognize their state and its location within the United States. Students may find it difficult to understand the concept of mental maps and may need a review each day. Students are not expected to define a mental map, but rather begin to understand how making pictures in their minds helps them to remember where things are located and what they look like. WEEK 1 1 Skill: Routes Essential Element 1: Standard 3 A Street Map of Parker Introducing the Map Ask students to name the street on which they live. T alk about how there are other words for street such as avenue, road, lane, and way. T ell students that no matter what the streets are called, they are all routes. Define route for students and discuss how vehicles such as trucks, cars, and buses follow different routes. Discuss with students how important it is to read a street map to find different places on a map. T alk about how confused people can get if they don’t follow a street map. Show students the street map of a small town called Parker. Read the title of the map. Point out the compass rose and talk about the directions. Name the different parts of the small town. Point out the youth center, the school, the park, and the post office. The students will also notice that there are houses or apartment buildings on almost every block. Read the street names in the town. Point out Main Street. T ell students that in many communities there is a Main Street, the most important street. This may have been the first street built in the community, or it may be where there are stores and businesses. T alk about how the street in this community runs north and south and the avenues all run east and west. Ask students where the Youth Center is located. WEEK 12 Skill: Routes Essential Element 1: Standard 3 A Road Map of Nebraska Introducing the Map Explain to students that a route is a way to go from one place to another. T ell students that there are many different types of routes. Discuss different transportation routes such as bike paths, streets, and highways. Ask students to think about a familiar route. T ell students that a route can be as simple as the way they walk to the mailbox every day. As a class, discuss familiar routes in your town or city. Have students look at the road map of Nebraska. Explain to students that this road map shows highways that are used for transportation. T ell students that there are two types of highways on the map. They are interstate and U.S. highways. Look at the map key to see the symbols for both kinds of highways. Point out the compass rose and talk about the directions. Have students follow Interstate 80 across the state, pointing out cities along the way. Then follow U.S. Highway 20 across the state, naming cities along the way. Students should notice from the key and the map that the symbol for a city is a dot. Ask students to identify the capital of Nebraska (Lincoln). Ask them on which highway Lincoln is located (Interstate 80). Share with students that only a few highways and cities are shown on this map. Review vocabulary throughout the week. Introducing Vocabulary highway A highway is a main road. Cars, trucks, and buses use highways to travel from one place to another. road map A road map shows highways people travel on. route A route is a way to go from one place to another. WEEK 13 Skill: Physical Features Essential Element 2: Standard 4 A World Map Introducing the Map Show the classroom globe to the students. T alk about how the globe shows the world or all of Earth. The globe shows the land and water on Earth. Then show students the classroom map of the world. T alk about how it is a flat picture of Earth. The world map shows all the land and water on Earth. Show students the world map from the book. T alk about how the world is divided into seven large land areas called continents. Name and locate the seven continents of the world. Help students to notice the shapes and sizes of the continents. Share with students the following information to help them to remember the seven continents. • Four of the continents start with the letter “A.” • Africa “hangs off” Europe and Asia. • Antarctica is the coldest and iciest place on Earth. Antarctica is located the farthest south. • Asia is the largest continent in size, and it has the most people. • Australia is an island continent. • North and South America have “America” in their names. North America is north of South America. South America is south of North America. • Sizes of continents from largest to smallest are: 1. Asia 5. Antarctica 2. Africa 6. Europe 3. North America 7. Australia 4. South America • Europe is joined to Asia in one large land area. D iscuss with students that the waters of the world are connected. The continents divide the waters into five parts. They are called oceans. The world has five oceans—Arctic, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Pacific. Review the vocabulary throughout the week. Continents and oceans are also defined in Weeks 1 and 2. Introducing Vocabulary border A border shows where places begin and end. A border can be a line on a map between states or countries. continent A continent is one of the seven very large areas of land on Earth. North America is a continent. ocean An ocean is a large body of salt water. Earth has five oceans. world The world is another name for Earth. The National Geography Standards The National Geography Standards includes six essential elements that highlight the major components of geography. Under the six major categories are the eighteen standards that focus on general areas in geography that children are expected to know and understand. Essential Element 1: The World in Spatial Terms Geography studies the relationships between people, places, and environments by mapping information about them into a spatial context. The geographically informed person knows and understands the following: Standard 1 ....................................................... Weeks 1–8 how to use maps and other geographic representations, tools, and technologies to acquire, process, and report information from a spatial perspective, Standard 2 ..................................................... Weeks 9–10 how to use mental maps to organize information about people, places, and environments in a spatial context, and Standard 3 .................................................... Weeks 11–12 how to analyze the spatial organization of people, places, and environments on Earth’s surface. Essential Element 2: Places and Regions The identities and lives of individuals and peoples are rooted in particular places and in those human constructs called regions. The geographically informed person knows and understands the following: Standard 4 .................................................... Weeks 13–18 the physical and human characteristics of places, Standard 5 .................................................... Weeks 19–22 that people create regions to interpret Earth’s complexity, and Standard 6 .................................................... Weeks 23–24 how culture and experience influence people’s perceptions of places and regions. Essential Element 3: Physical Systems Physical processes shape Earth’s surface and interact with plant and animal life to create, sustain, and modify the ecosystems. The geographically informed person knows and understands the following: Standard 7 ........................................................ Week 25 the physical processes that shape the patterns of Earth’s surface, and Standard 8 ......................................................... Week 26 the characteristics and spatial distribution of ecosystems on Earth’s surface. 3711BookNoTransp.indb 4 9/21/12 9:43 AM

WEEK 19 Skill: Political Regions Essential Element 2: Standard 5 A Rural Area Map Introducing the Map Share with students that there are different kinds of communities. T ell students that most people today live in large cities. But long ago, most of the people lived on small farms or in very small communities. The farm families raised their own cows, chickens, and pigs. They grew their own corn, wheat, fruits, and garden vegetables. Most farm families produced enough food for themselves. Later, better kinds of plants and better ways of growing crops were developed. Methods of raising animals were developed. Modern farm equipment was invented, so fewer people were needed to work on farms. The changes in farming in the United States also led to the growth of cities and towns. Because fewer people were needed to produce food, many people moved to towns and cities. T oday in the United States, fewer than 3 of every 100 people live on farms. But the people who do live on farms now can produce enough food to feed the world. Each farmer today can produce enough food to feed more than 80 people. That is why farming communities are very important. Share with students that farming communities are also called rural areas. Show students the map of a rural area. T wo farms are shown on the map. T ell students that in rural areas there is a lot of land and few people. T alk about how a county road used to be called a “farm to market” road. Farmers took their products to nearby towns to sell. This is still done, but large trucks now carry the farm products to factories in towns and cities. Also, talk about the advantages and disadvantages of living in a rural area. This lesson will help students to understand one kind of region. Weeks 20 and 21 focus on suburbs and larger cities. Review vocabulary throughout the week to check for understanding. Introducing Vocabulary community A community is a group of people who live together in the same area. countryside Countryside is land away from cities and towns. farm A farm is land that a farmer uses to grow crops or raise animals. rural area A rural area is a farming community or the countryside. WEEK 20 Skill: Political Regions Essential Element 2: Standard 5 A Suburb Map Introducing the Map Share with students that there are different kinds of communities. In Week 19, a rural community was highlighted. T ell students that almost half of the people in the United States live in communities called suburbs. Suburbs are communities near big cities. As cities grew more and more crowded, people started building houses farther away from the city. Suburbs were created. Originally, suburbs were mostly made up of homes with a few businesses nearby. People commuted from their homes in the suburbs to the city to work. Now suburbs are the fastest growing communities. Suburbs have many housing developments. The houses tend to be newer and are grouped together along streets. Many of the houses have nice-sized yards. There are shopping malls, businesses, and offices in suburbs. People live and work in suburbs. Some people still travel from the suburbs to work in the nearby city. Show students the map of a suburb. Read the caption with students to find out the names of the suburb and big city that are on the map. T alk about the parts of the suburb. Read the stores that are along Lake Street. Students should notice that a major road leads from the suburb to the city. In this lesson, students should begin to understand the concept of a suburb. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of living in a suburb. Review vocabulary throughout the week to check for understanding. Introducing Vocabulary city A city is a large or important town. A dot on a map shows where a city is found. community A community is a group of people who live together in the same area. suburb A suburb is a community near a city. ANSWER KEY Monday 1. suburb 2. a city Tuesday 1. Elgin 2. Chicago Wednesday 1. houses 2. Lake Street Thursday 1. Willow Road 2. WEEK 21 Skill: Political Regions Essential Element 2: Standard 5 A City Map Introducing the Map Share with students that there are different kinds of communities. In Weeks 19 and 20, a rural area and then a suburb were highlighted. Another kind of community is a city. T ell students that a city is a community where thousands or even millions of people live and work. A city is a crowded place. Show students the map of a city. Discuss with students how many large cities have a central section called the downtown area. In the downtown area, there are things like banks, department stores, museums, restaurants, and big companies. Some of the companies are in skyscrapers that tower over the busy streets of a city. Large apartment buildings can also be found in this area. T alk about how many people in a city use public transportation such as buses, subways, and trains to get around the city. Point out the different areas of the downtown area on the city map. Further explain to students that most people’s homes are located in neighborhoods outside of the downtown area. Outside of the downtown area of a city, you would also find areas that have big factories that make products such as clothes, tools, and cars. Big airports may be found in this area, too. Sometimes an airport is located near downtown. In this lesson, students should begin to understand the concept of a big city and how busy and crowded it can be. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of living in a big city. People find it exciting to live where there are tall skyscrapers, museums, giant sports stadiums, and job opportunities. Others find living in a city harder because it is so crowded and noisy. Review vocabulary throughout the week to check for understanding. Introducing Vocabulary city A city is a large or important town. A dot on a map shows where a city is found. community A community is a group of people who live together in the same area. downtown Downtown is a city’s main business area. skyscraper A skyscraper is a very tall building. WEEK 23 Skill: Cultural Landmarks Essential Element 2: Standard 6 An Amusement Park Introducing the Map Ask students to name a special place they would like to go on vacation. Many students will say Disneyland or Disneyworld. That is because amusement parks have become important landmarks in American culture. Define amusement parks for students and talk about why families like to visit them. T ell students that the word amuse means “to make someone laugh or smile.” It also means “to keep someone happy and stop him or her from being bored.” Share with students that amusement parks have been around for over 400 years. The first amusement parks were called “Pleasure Gardens.” The gardens were filled with games, music, and the first amusement rides. The roller coaster and the Ferris wheel were two of the first amusement rides to be invented. Amusement parks grew in popularity with the invention of more and more rides. Share with students that Disneyland opened in 1955. It was called an amusement park, but it was also called a theme park. A theme park has rides and games, but it is based on a subject, such as space travel. Disneyland’s theme was “The Magic Kingdom.” This kind of park appeals to the whole family. Now amusement parks are all over the country. When families think about a fun family vacation, they often think of going to amusement parks. Share with students that when people are asked to name a famous landmark in the United States, people say “Disneyland” more often than other famous landmarks like Mount Rushmore or the Statue of Liberty. That is how popular amusement parks have become in the world. Show students the map of the amusement park. Read and discuss the areas of the park. Review vocabulary with students throughout the week. Introducing Vocabulary amusement park An amusement park is a place where people pay to get in. People go on rides, play games, and enjoy shows. Disneyland is an amusement park. entrance An entrance is a way into a place. exit An exit is a way out of a place. landmark A landmark is an important place or building. Mount Rushmore is a landmark. theme park A theme park is an amusement park with a theme, like space travel. Theme parks have rides and games. Disneyland is a theme park. ANSWER KEY Monday 1. an amusement 2. 6 rides Tuesday 1. Any three of the following: bumper cars, Ferris wheel, log ride, merry-go-round, roller coaster, or train ride 2. in the middle Wednesday 1. log ride 2. roller coaster Thursday 1. merry-go-round and train ride 2. roller coaster Friday 1. bumper cars and gift shop 2. the entrance Challenge Answers will var y. You may wish to brainstorm ideas as a class before students choose their favorite names of the park. Students should color their new amusement park. 3711BookNoTransp.indb 94 9/21/12 9:43 AM

content.passage: Who We Are • At Evan-Moor, we are proud that our products are written, edited, and tested by professional educators. • Evan-Moor’s materials are directed to teachers and parents of prekindergarten through sixth-grade students. • We address all major curriculum areas, including: reading social studies thematic units writing geography arts & crafts math science How We Began • In 1979, Joy Evans and Jo Ellen Moore were team-teaching ﬁrst grade in a Title I school. They decided to put ideas that worked for their students into a book. They joined with Bill Evans (Joy’s brother) to start Evan-Moor Educational Publishers with one book. • Bill and Joy’s parents’ garage served as the warehouse and shipping facility. • The ﬁrst catalog was a folded 8 ½" x 11" sheet of paper! Who We Became • Evan-Moor now offers over 450 titles. Our materials can be found in over 1,500 educational and trade book stores around the world. • We mail almost 2 million catalogs a year to schools and individual teachers. • Our Web site www.evan-moor.com offers 24-hour service and the ability to download many of our titles. • Evan-Moor is located in a 20,000-square-foot facility in Monterey, California, with a staff of nearly 60 professionals. Our Mission Now, as then, we are dedicated to helping children learn. We think it is the world’s most important job, and we strive to assist teachers and parents in this essential endeavor. content.passage: 2 EMC 751 • © Evan-Moor Corp. You may want to use all of the following presentations throughout the year to keep each lesson fresh and interesting. 1. Make overhead transparencies of the lessons. Present each lesson as an oral activity with the entire class. Write answers and make corrections using an erasable marker. As the class becomes more familiar with Daily Math Practice, you may want students to mark their answers ﬁrst and then check them against correct responses marked on the transparency. 2. Reproduce the pages for individuals or partners to work on independently. Check answers as a group, using an overhead transparency to model the correct answers. (Use these pages as independent practice only after much oral group experience with the lessons.) 3. Occasionally you may want to use a day’s or even a full week’s lesson(s) as a test to see how individuals are progressing in their acquisition of skills. Some Important Considerations 1. Allow students to use whatever tools they need to solve problems. Some students will choose to use manipulatives, while others will want to make drawings. 2. It is important that students be able to share their solutions. This modeling of a variety of problem-solving techniques provides a great learning beneﬁt. Don ’t scrimp on the amount of time you allow for discussing how solutions were reached. Suggestions and Options 1. Sometimes you will not have taught a given skill before it appears in a lesson. These items should then be done together. Tell the class that you are going to work on a skill they have not yet been taught. Use the practice time to conduct a minilesson on that skill. 2. Customize the daily lessons to the needs of your class. • If there are skills that are not included in the grade-level expectancies of the particular program you teach, you may choose to skip those items. • If you feel your class needs more practice than is provided, add these “extras” on your own in the form of a one-item warm-up or posttest. content.passage: 2 EMC 752 • © Evan-Moor Corp. You may want to use all of the following presentations throughout the year to keep each lesson fresh and interesting. 1 . Make overhead transparencies of the lessons. Present each lesson as an oral activity with the entire class. Write answers and make corrections using an erasable marker. As the class becomes more familiar with Daily Math Practice, you may want students to mark their answers ﬁrst and then check them against correct responses marked on the transparency. 2. Reproduce the pages for individuals or partners to work on independently. Check answers as a group, using an overhead transparency to model the correct answers. (Use these pages as independent practice only after much oral group experience with the lessons.) 3. Occasionally you may want to use a day ʼs or even a full weekʼs lesson(s) as a test to see how individuals are progressing in their acquisition of skills. Some Important Considerations 1 . Allow students to use whatever tools they need to solve problems. Some students will choose to use manipulatives, while others will want to make drawings. 2. It is important that students be able to share their solutions. This modeling of a variety of problem-solving techniques provides a great learning beneﬁt. Don ʼt scrimp on the amount of time you allow for discussing how solutions were reached. 3. With the focus of the ﬁrst four days being on computation and problem solving, it is recommended that calculators be used only on Fridays, when the focus is much more detailed, with less emphasis on computation. In some instances, however, you may want to allow the use of calculators to solve the daily word problems. Suggestions and Options 1 . Sometimes you will not have taught a given skill before it appears in a lesson. These items should then be done together. Tell the class that you are going to work on a skill they have not yet been taught. Use the practice time to conduct a minilesson on that skill. 2. Customize the daily lessons to the needs of your class. • If there are skills that are not included in the grade-level expectancies of the particular program you teach, you may choose to skip those items. • If you feel your class needs more practice than is provided, add these “extras” on your own in the form of a one-item warm-up or posttest. 3. Many of the Friday problems are quite challenging and lend themselves to partner or small-group collaboration. How to Use Daily Math Practice

content.passage: 2 Daily Language Review, Grade 4 • EMC 582 • ©2004 Evan-Moor Corp. How to Use Daily Language Review There are several ways that the daily review practices can be presented. You may want to use all of these presentations throughout the year to help keep the practice fresh and interesting. Make overhead transparencies of the lessons. Conduct the practice as an oral activity with the entire class. Write answers and make corrections using an erasable pen. Increased retention of the skill will occur if students mark the answers at the same time on a reproduced sheet or write the answers on writing paper. As the class becomes more familiar with Daily Language Review, you may want students to mark their own answers ﬁrst and then check responses by marking the items on the transparency. Reproduce the pages for individuals or partners to work independently. Check answers as a group, using an overhead transparency to model the correct answers. Use these pages as independent practice only after much oral group experience with the lessons. Occasionally you may want to use a day’s, or even a week’s, lesson as a test to see how individuals are progressing in their acquisition of skills. It should be stressed, however, that the greatest learning beneﬁt will be gained from doing the practices orally so that students continually hear correct responses modeled by their class- mates and the teacher. Hints, Suggestions, and Options 1. Look ahead several weeks at the skills being practiced. If possible, teach new skills in formal lessons before asking students to practice these skills in the daily review. 2. Sometimes you will not have taught a given skill before it appears in a lesson. These items should then be done together. Tell the class that there is a skill they have not yet been taught. See if anyone knows the answer and wishes to explain it to the class. If not, use the review time to conduct a minilesson on that skill. 3. Customize the daily review lessons to the needs of your class. • If there are skills that are not included in the grade-level expectancies of the particular program you teach, you may choose to skip those items—white them out or correct them before reproducing the page. • If you feel your class needs more practice than is provided, add these “extras” on your own. For example: Use the daily “edit” sentences to locate subject, predicate, parts of speech, etc. Add a one-item warm-up, a mini-posttest, or ask students to provide another example. 3 1 2

content.passage: 2 EMC 753 • © Evan-Moor Corp. You may want to use all of the following presentations throughout the year to keep each lesson fresh and interesting. 1. Make overhead transparencies of the lessons. Present each lesson as an oral activity with the entire class. Write answers and make corrections using an erasable marker. As the class becomes more familiar with Daily Math Practice, you may want students to mark their answers ﬁrst and then check them against correct responses marked on the transparency. 2. Reproduce the pages for individuals or partners to work on independently. Check answers as a group, using an overhead transparency to model the correct answers. (Use these pages as independent practice only after much oral group experience with the lessons.) 3. Occasionally you may want to use a dayʼs or even a full weekʼs lesson(s) as a test to see how individuals are progressing in their acquisition of skills. Some Important Considerations 1. Allow students to use whatever tools they need to solve problems. Some students will choose to use manipulatives, while others will want to make drawings. 2. It is important that students be able to share their solutions. This modeling of a variety of problem-solving techniques provides a great learning beneﬁt. Don ʼt scrimp on the amount of time you allow for discussing how solutions were reached. 3. With the focus of the ﬁrst four days being on computation and problem solving, it is recommended that calculators be used only on Fridays, when the focus is much more detailed, with less emphasis on computation. In some instances, however, you may want to allow the use of calculators to solve the daily word problems. Suggestions and Options 1. Sometimes you will not have taught a given skill before it appears in a lesson. These items should then be done together. Tell the class that you are going to work on a skill they have not yet been taught. Use the practice time to conduct a minilesson on that skill. 2. Customize the daily lessons to the needs of your class. • If there are skills that are not included in the grade-level expectancies of the particular program you teach, you may choose to skip those items. • If you feel your class needs more practice than is provided, add these “extras” on your own in the form of a one-item warm-up or posttest. 3. Many of the Friday problems are quite challenging and lend themselves to partner or small-group collaboration. How to Use Daily Math Practice

content.passage: 2 EMC 754 • © Evan-Moor Corp. How to Use Daily Math Practice You may want to use all of the following presentations throughout the year to keep each lesson fresh and interesting. 1 . Make overhead transparencies of the lessons. Present each lesson as an oral activity with the entire class. Write answers and make corrections using an erasable marker. As the class becomes more familiar with Daily Math Practice, you may want students to mark their answers ﬁrst and then check them against correct responses marked on the transparency. 2. Reproduce the pages for individuals or partners to work on independently. Check answers as a group, using an overhead transparency to model the correct answers. (Use these pages as independent practice only after much oral group experience with the lessons.) 3. Occasionally you may want to use a day ʼs or even a full weekʼs lesson(s) as a test to see how individuals are progressing in their acquisition of skills. Some Important Considerations 1 . Allow students to use whatever tools they need to solve problems. Some students will choose to use manipulatives, while others will want to make drawings. 2. It is important that students be able to share their solutions. This modeling of a variety of problem-solving techniques provides a great learning beneﬁt. Don ʼt scrimp on the amount of time you allow for discussing how solutions were reached. 3. With the focus of the ﬁrst four days being on computation and problem solving, it is recommended that calculators be used only on Fridays, when the focus is much more detailed, with less emphasis on computation. In some instances, however, you may want to allow the use of calculators to solve the daily word problems. Suggestions and Options 1 . Sometimes you will not have taught a given skill before it appears in a lesson. These items should then be done together. Tell the class that you are going to work on a skill they have not yet been taught. Use the practice time to conduct a minilesson on that skill. 2. Customize the daily lessons to the needs of your class. • If there are skills that are not included in the grade-level expectancies of the particular program you teach, you may choose to skip those items. • If you feel your class needs more practice than is provided, add these “extras” on your own in the form of a one-item warm-up or posttest. 3. Many of the Friday problems are quite challenging and lend themselves to partner or small-group collaboration.

Guide dogs are trained to help the blind navigate crowded buildings and city streets. But dogs, and even monkeys, are trained to happily perform many other tasks. Hearing dogs are trained to alert their deaf handlers to important sounds. They know telephone rings, smoke alarms, and sirens. They can even recall the deaf person’s name. The dog swiftly alerts the handler by pawing and then leading him or her to the sound. Service animals, such as dogs and monkeys, help handlers who are conﬁ ned to wheelchairs. The animals can pull the chairs, turn lights on and off, and open doors. They can also push elevator buttons and pick up or carry objects. Most of all, they help handlers rebuild their lives. Some people in wheelchairs are unable to move their arms or legs. Capuchin monkeys are trained as helpers because their hands are like human hands. Monkeys can brush hair, serve food, and do housework. They can even help with CDs and videos! Service animals act as tireless friends. The special bond between animal and handler is unlike any other.

Many people used to think that comets were on ﬁ re. Now we know that comets are frozen lumps of ice and dust. They enter our solar system from far away. When a comet gets close to the sun, the sun’s heat vaporizes some of the comet. Gas and dust are released and form long sunlit tails that follow the comet. We can see these beautiful tails, which can be millions of miles long, from Earth. Comet comes from a Greek word meaning “long-haired star.” This is because the tail of the comet looks like ﬂ owing hair. The most famous comet is Halley’s comet. Reports of this comet date back more than 2,200 years! Halley’s comet makes its usual visit every 76 years. If you want to see Halley’s comet, you’ll have to wait a long time. It won’t visit Earth again until 2061, many years in the future.

Check off the words you can find in the story. ancient oath heroes swore brother holiday athlete mountain month July August summer How many spelling words did you find ? ______ ©2005 by Evan-Moor Corp. • EMC 4540 • Spell & Write UNIT 3 23 The Greeks Were First The Olympic Games have been around a long time! The ancient games began in Greece in 776 B.C. At ﬁ rst, the games were a holiday in honor of Zeus. He was the father of all the Greek gods. The games were held at Mt. Olympus, the highest mountain in Greece. They took place every fourth summer in July or August. Athletes did not compete on teams, but as individuals. Only men and boys could compete. They trained for ten long months. Before the games began, they swore an oath of honesty. Their fathers and brothers had to swear the same oath. Some events were similar to today’s events. There were foot races, wrestling, boxing, jumping, and javelin throwing. There were also different events, such as chariot races. The biggest difference was the dress. Athletes competed without clothes! Winners did not get medals. Instead, they were given wreaths of olive leaves. Winning athletes were hailed as great heroes. They became rich and famous. Poems and sculptures were created in their honor. Where were the women and girls? Women were not allowed to compete. They weren’t even allowed to watch! There was another festival to honor Hera, the wife of Zeus. That event had foot races for unmarried girls.
